clue.text: Portion of money from large farm in borders of Tennessee

indicators.note: in says the farm goes inside the state's border letters
the borders of a word are its first and last letters

parts.note: the word whose outer letters are taken
a ranch is a large farm, especially for cattle

explanation.surface: Someone takes a share of the money made on a big Tennessee farm.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennessee is not the state here, only a source of its two edge letters; 'from' simply links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A tranche is an instalment or slice of a larger sum, as when a loan is released in tranches.

clue.text: Furry creature hurried around cricket club and pool essentially

indicators.note: the hurrying word goes round the others

parts.note: ran = hurried
standard abbreviation

indicators.note: the essence of a word is its middle

parts.note: middle letters of POOL

explanation.surface: An animal dashes around a cricket ground and its swimming pool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pool essentially' looks like a word for water; it means the core of the word POOL.
explanation.definitionFit: A raccoon is a North American mammal with a thick, ringed, furry coat.

clue.text: Impractical time in middle of day

parts.note: noon is midday
T = time, as in physics

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles that a midday appointment is simply unworkable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Middle of day' looks like an instruction to take the middle letter of DAY; it is simply NOON.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Not on' is British slang for unacceptable or impractical, as in 'That plan's just not on.'

clue.text: Trendy sort in joint getting sun on terrace

indicators.note: the joint acquires what follows
in a down clue, on means placed above

parts.note: the hip is a joint
S = sun
Ter. is the address abbreviation for Terrace

explanation.surface: A fashionable type sunbathes on the terrace of a bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint' tempts as a bar or pub, which fits the scene; here it is the body's hip.
explanation.definitionFit: A hipster is someone who follows the latest trends, a trendy sort.

clue.text: Diver at sea going round lake with Yankee showing mischief

indicators.note: with adds the letter for Yankee alongside, at the end
going round says the rearranged letters surround the letter for lake
at sea means confused, so the letters of Diver are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written: the letters to rearrange
L is a standard map abbreviation for lake
Yankee is the NATO phonetic alphabet word for Y

explanation.surface: A diver swimming in the sea circles a lake with an American companion, causing trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at sea' rearranges DIVER into DEVIR, which goes 'round' L before Y is added. 'Diver at sea' paints a scene, but 'at sea' is the rearrangement signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Devilry is wicked or reckless behaviour, playful or otherwise, which is a form of mischief.

clue.text: Liken opening of enquiry with question at issue lately

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter of ENQUIRY
QU is a standard abbreviation for question
taken as written

indicators.note: late in the word means its last letter

parts.note: last letter of ISSUE

explanation.surface: An inquiry keeps comparing things as the question has become contentious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At issue' reads as a single phrase; split it, and AT is used as written while 'issue lately' gives only E.
explanation.definitionFit: To equate two things is to liken them, treating them as equal.

clue.text: Complicated act in rite when reviewed

indicators.note: to review is to look again and rework, so the letters are reorganised

parts.note: the nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A ceremonial performance turns out to be elaborate once someone reviews it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reviewed' suggests writing a critique of the performance, but here it only signals rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Intricate means complicated, full of fine interlocking detail.

clue.text: Four on island in unusually rare coastal region

indicators.note: in says the numeral and island go inside the jumbled letters
unusually means not in the normal way, so the letters of rare are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written: the letters to rearrange

indicators.note: on places the numeral against the island letter in a single run

parts.note: IV is four in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Four people stranded on an island in an exotic coastal area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusually' jumbles the four letters so they split around the numeral and island, which sit 'in' them. The Riviera is the Mediterranean coast of south-east France and north-west Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: The Riviera is a stretch of Mediterranean coastline, and the word is used for any fashionable seaside strip.

clue.text: Ongoing relief devised for corps recruiting volunteers

indicators.note: to devise is to work up something new, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the thirteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A continuing aid scheme has been set up for soldiers who signed on freely.
explanation.walkthrough: The French Foreign Legion is a military corps that recruits volunteers of any nationality.
explanation.definitionFit: The Foreign Legion is a corps made up entirely of volunteer enlistees.

clue.text: Rabbit's tail is cutesy? Not entirely

indicators.note: the answer is only part of the words in front

parts.note: the letters straddle the end of 'is' and the start of 'cutesy'

explanation.surface: Someone asks, doubtfully, whether a bunny's tail really counts as cute.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark keeps the surface a chatty aside, so 'Not entirely' reads as a verdict rather than an instruction; the answer is iS CUTesy.
explanation.definitionFit: A scut is the short, upright tail of a rabbit, hare or deer.

clue.text: Efficient person that's paid by channel I have contracted

definitions.note: 'Efficient person' reads as a noun, but only 'Efficient' is the definition, an adjective like the answer.

indicators.note: I HAVE shortened, as in the contraction I've

parts.note: a pro is a professional, paid for their work
a duct is a channel
I've, without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A capable worker has signed a deal with a TV channel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Channel' and 'contracted' conjure a broadcaster's employment deal; the channel is a pipe and the contract is an apostrophe.
explanation.definitionFit: Productive means getting a lot done, efficient.

clue.text: Younger relative recalled figure in short poem

parts.note: a son is younger than his parent

indicators.note: called back, so the number is turned round

parts.note: a figure is a number

explanation.surface: A youngster remembers a character from a little poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Figure' looks like a person in the poem; it is a number.
explanation.definitionFit: A sonnet is a fourteen-line poem, short by any standard.

clue.text: Counterpart in awful need getting in a tangle?

indicators.note: in says the counterpart goes inside the jumbled letters
awful means very bad, so the word need comes out in a disordered form

parts.note: taken as written: the letters to rearrange
a twin is a counterpart, one of a matching pair

explanation.surface: A double in desperate need gets themselves into a mess.
explanation.walkthrough: The jumbled letters wrap around the counterpart, which sits 'in' them; 'getting' only links the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that are entwined are twisted or wound together, which is to say they are tangled up.

clue.text: Egg on new firm in multinational group with fancy gear

indicators.note: with puts the rearranged gear alongside, at the end
in says the new firm sits inside the abbreviation for the group

parts.note: EU, the European Union, is a group of many nations
CO is the abbreviation for company, a firm

indicators.note: fancy means elaborate or imaginative, so the letters of gear are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A start-up joins a European trade bloc and kits itself out in smart equipment.
explanation.walkthrough: Egg here is the verb, to urge, not the food. 'fancy' turns GEAR into RAGE.
explanation.definitionFit: To egg someone on is to urge or spur them, which means much the same as to encourage them.

clue.text: Article probing performing chaps given day in recovery?

indicators.note: given, in the sense of granted an extra, adds the letter for day at the end
probing means poking inside, so the article goes into the middle of the other letters

parts.note: an act that is performing is on, as in on stage
chaps are men
the is the definite article

explanation.surface: A newspaper article investigates male performers who are given a day off to recuperate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' is the grammar word, not a newspaper piece; 'probing' pushes it between performing and chaps, and the day is 'given' at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone on the mend is getting better after an illness or injury, so is recovering.

clue.text: People hail this US gangster in intriguing faction

parts.note: you hail a cab
Al Capone, the Chicago gangster

explanation.surface: Crowds cheer an American mobster who belongs to a plotting gang.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hail' suggests cheering or saluting the gangster; it is flagging down a taxi. Crosswords use AL for the gangster Al Capone.
explanation.definitionFit: A cabal is a small secret group plotting together, an intriguing faction.

clue.text: Ill-feeling produced by dirty venue in the Kent area

indicators.note: the venue sits inside the area

parts.note: Kent is a county in south-east England
a pit is a grim, dirty place

explanation.surface: Resentment is stirred up by a grubby venue somewhere in Kent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Kent area' needs geography: Kent is in the south-east of England, so SE.
explanation.definitionFit: Spite is malicious ill-feeling towards someone.

clue.text: Standard note found in a large thing supplying shade

parts.note: par is the standard

indicators.note: the note is inside the next letters

parts.note: A plus L for large
the note so (soh) in do-re-mi

explanation.surface: A standard note is found in a big object that gives shade.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is only loosely a picture; the value is in splitting 'a large' into A and L.
explanation.definitionFit: A parasol is a light umbrella giving shade from the sun.

clue.text: Having a complaint, a guy is uncomfortable

parts.note: a complaint is an illness
taken as written
to guy someone is to mock or tease them

explanation.surface: A man with a grievance feels awkward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guy' reads as a man; it is the verb meaning to make fun of, and TEASE also works as a noun for a joker.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the phrase describes feeling awkward or anxious, not physical discomfort.

clue.text: A loser sadly pocketing nothing for spray can

indicators.note: pocketing means putting into a pocket, so the rearranged letters hold the letter for nothing
sadly signals the letters are put into a sorry state, rearranged

parts.note: taken as written: letters to rearrange with A
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A miserable failure pockets nothing and settles for a can of spray paint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sadly' rearranges A LOSER, which goes round O, 'pocketing' it. The surface makes a story of a loser, but those words are just letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An aerosol is a pressurised container that releases its contents as a fine mist, so a spray can.

clue.text: Safekeeping adopted by artist or agent

indicators.note: taken in and held by the following words

parts.note: the letters run from the end of 'artist' through 'or' into 'agent'

explanation.surface: An artist or their agent takes charge of looking after the paintings.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer spans all three words, artiST OR AGEnt, which is why 'adopted by' covers the whole phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Storage is keeping things safe until needed, safekeeping.

clue.text: Link including instruction to reader to walk quietly

indicators.note: the link takes the instruction inside it

parts.note: a tie links things
PTO, please turn over, at the foot of a page

explanation.surface: A connection comes with a note telling the reader to creep along.
explanation.walkthrough: PTO is 'please turn over', printed at the bottom of a page.
explanation.definitionFit: To tiptoe is to walk quietly on the tips of one's toes.

clue.text: Salutation in Greek assembly after missing start

indicators.note: the word loses its first letter

parts.note: GR is the abbreviation for Greek
MEETING without its first letter

explanation.surface: A welcome speech at a Greek meeting that got off to a false start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' makes the salutation seem to happen in the assembly; it is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: salutation is the formal word for saying hello or waving to someone.

clue.text: Motive concerning a disciple

parts.note: re = concerning, about
taken as written
a disciple can be called a son of his master

explanation.surface: An investigator looks for the motive behind a follower's actions.
explanation.walkthrough: SON for disciple is a stretch: think of a devoted follower as a spiritual son.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words name what drives someone to act.

clue.text: Book of maps finally reduced

indicators.note: reduced says the phrase is made shorter, losing its last letter

parts.note: finally means at last

explanation.surface: A bookshop's maps have at last been marked down in price.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally' looks like a letter-picking signal for a final letter, but it is a synonym: AT LAST, which 'reduced' shortens.
explanation.definitionFit: An atlas is a bound collection of maps, a volume of charts of the world or a region.

clue.text: Senator is upset facing first of such claims

indicators.note: facing puts the jumbled letters up against the one taken from such, ahead of it
upset means knocked over and disordered, so the letters of Senator and is are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written: letters to rearrange
taken as written: letters to rearrange

indicators.note: first of picks the opening letter

parts.note: the word whose opening letter is taken

explanation.surface: An irritated politician confronts the first of a set of allegations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Senator' looks like the subject of the sentence, but with 'is' it is only letters for 'upset' to jumble; 'facing' puts them before the letter from 'first of such'.
explanation.definitionFit: Assertions are confident statements of fact or belief, which is what claims are.

clue.text: Miserable bishop going off to make unauthorised disclosure

indicators.note: the bishop leaves the word

parts.note: bleak = miserable
B = bishop, as in chess notation

explanation.surface: An unhappy bishop storms off to tip off the press.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a church scandal; the bishop is only the letter B leaving BLEAK.
explanation.definitionFit: To leak information is to disclose it without permission.

clue.text: One working slowly in place of more peculiar character

parts.note: PL is the address abbreviation for Place
odder = more peculiar; 'character' is surface dressing for the adjective

explanation.surface: A slow worker stands in for a stranger character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In place of' reads as 'instead of'; break it up, and 'place' is simply PL followed by ODDER.
explanation.definitionFit: A plodder is someone who works slowly and steadily.

clue.text: Bunch caught by unexpected result

indicators.note: by places the letter for caught beside the rearranged result, here in front

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

indicators.note: unexpected means not as predicted, so the letters of result come out jumbled

parts.note: taken as written: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A batsman's dismissal, caught, brings a surprising outcome to a cricket match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unexpected' rearranges RESULT into LUSTER after C. In cricket scorecards C stands for caught.
explanation.definitionFit: A cluster is a group of similar things close together, such as a bunch of grapes.
